newsitem.title: ITALY: Arrested Italian rail chief quits board.
newsitem.headline: Arrested Italian rail chief quits board.

text.p: The managing director of Italy's state railway, Lorenzo Necci, resigned his post on Thursday in a letter written from the prison cell where he is being held on suspicion of committing a raft of corruption-related offences.
The resignation was announced by Necci's lawyers just hours before the board of the company, Ferrovie dello Stato, was due to meet to discuss the fallout from his dramatic arrest.

It coincided with parliamentary soul-searching on how much of a lesson in honesty Italy had learned from four years of devastating corruption scandals which toppled the post-World War Two political establishment.
Necci, 55, was arrested on September 15 on the orders of magistrates in the northwest town of La Spezia investigating an alleged corrupt "super lobby" in state industries and the judiciary.
Necci, in a letter written by hand, said he had resigned as managing director and from the board "with immediate effect".
The letter, a copy of which was released to the media, defended Necci's six-year record at the railroad but made no direct reference to the case against him.

It was not immediately clear who will replace Necci at Ferrovie dello Stato, which is pursuing a planned multi-billion dollar project championed by the disgraced executive to build a new high-speed rail system.
The centre-left government has already said it intends to appoint an outsider to the job.

One man tipped by newspapers as a possible replacement, former budget minister Rainer Masera, said on Thursday that he was not interested in the post. Masera is director general of the privatised merchant bank IMI.
The Necci affair has mushroomed since his arrest to include judges, businessmen and lawyers as magistrates probe allegations of trial-fixing and widespread bribes for state contracts.
Newspapers have quickly dubbed the case "Tangentopoli 2", an echo of the "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) corruption scandal which exploded in 1992 and buried Italy's governing elite.

Politicians from government and opposition acknowledged on Thursday that the country still had to learn the lessons of the original scandal, including the need for greater accountability and supervision of public sector spending.
Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick, replying in a debate in the Senate (upper house) on corruption, said there were only two ways to emerge from Tangentopoli.
"Either you stop stealing or you erect obstacles in the path of people who steal to stop them," Flick said.

The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) also voted overwhemingly on Thursday to create a special all-party commission of 25 members with four months to draft proposals on the prevention and repression of graft in public life.
Only two deputies voted against setting up the commission, which was proposed by lower house Speaker Luciano Violante, a former leading magistrate.
One supporter, Pietro Folena of the Democratic Party of the Left, said the commission would allow parliament and politicians to regain the upper hand in the war on corruption.
"This will overcome the inertia of the past few years which has seen the fight against corruption delegated almost exclusively to magistrates," Folena told the 630-seat assembly.
